events.headline: China Burns Less Oil and Coal as the Iran War Reshapes Its Energy Mix

items.title: China Burns Less Oil and Coal as the Iran War Reshapes Its Energy Mix
items.summary: The war in Iran is causing an enduring upset in global oil and gas markets with long-ranging consequences for the economy, the energy sector, and the climate. events.article_text:
EU Delays Methane Rules by Two Years Amid Energy Supply Fears

Haley Zaremba is an energy journalist and researcher with more than a decade of professional experience covering global energy systems, land and natural resources, and…

The war in Iran is causing an enduring upset in global oil and gas markets with long-ranging consequences for the economy, the energy sector, and the climate. For many countries, this has resulted in skyrocketing energy prices and a rapid shift toward renewable energies in order to fill the import gap. For China, the global leader in clean energy supply chains by a massive margin, this has resulted in a windfall – and a drop in greenhouse gas emissions.

China has led global clean energy development for years now, spending more than the rest of the world combined on solar, wind, batteries, and other vital clean energy components. China still consumes vast amounts of fossil fuels and remains the world’s largest consumer of coal, but the massive buildout of cleaner alternatives has resulted in plateaued greenhouse gas emissions in recent years. And now, thanks to the impacts of the war in Iran, those emissions have started to dip.

In the third quarter of this year, China’s carbon dioxide emissions saw their biggest fall since the COVID pandemic, at a 3.1 percent decline between July and September. A major uptick in electric vehicle adoption drove much of this decline, as consumers reacted to skyrocketing oil prices by ditching conventional gas-burning engines. As a result, China’s oil consumption fell by 4 percent year-on-year.

Coal consumption also fell this year, although China continues to build new coal-fired plants. Emissions from the dirtiest fossil fuel fell by 3 percent year-on-year across the country thanks to the rapid buildout of renewable energy resources and comparatively slow growth of energy demand. “China added enough wind, solar, and nuclear generation over the same period to power Germany and more than twice as much as needed to meet China’s growing demand,” reports Yale 360. “Emissions from the production of steel and concrete also fell amid the ongoing construction slowdown.”

China’s huge clean energy push hasn’t just transformed its own energy sector – it’s catalyzing a clean energy shift around the world. Rich countries have continued a pivot toward clean energy as the latest oil and gas crisis has shown the vulnerabilities of relying on fossil fuel imports, while cash-poor developing economies are starting to adopt these technologies at a previously unseen pace. For these countries that suffer the most from energy market volatility, cheap Chinese solar panels and batteries present a critical lifeline.

“Some countries are pulling off stunningly fast energy transitions, adding solar so rapidly, it’s become a major source of electricity over the course of years — not decades,” CNN wrote in a report earlier this year. Indeed, Pakistan has become the surprise poster child of solar-plus-battery system growth as residents install rooftop solar and batteries faster than any other market on Earth. And Pakistan is not alone – emerging economies including Brazil, Chile, El Salvador, Morocco, Kenya, and Namibia have all overtaken the United States – the world’s largest economy – in their clean energy transitions.

Increasingly, clean energy represents energy security and affordability as much or more than it represents sustainability. “Wind and solar cannot be embargoed, blockaded, or shut off by a foreign power,” David Frykman, General Partner at Stockholm-based venture capital group Norrsken, wrote in an op-ed for Fortune earlier this year. “Every terawatt-hour of domestic renewable generation is a terawatt-hour that no adversary can weaponize.” Plus, solar and wind have simply become too cheap to fail, in large part thanks to China’s manufacturing bonanza.

And experts say that we can expect to see these trends continue in the coming years. “This is part of a longer trend, not just an immediate response to higher oil and gas prices,” said Yang Biqing, a China analyst at London-based energy think tank Ember, in an interview with the Washington Post. “Energy security is becoming more important on governments’ agenda, and the shift toward clean energy is increasingly being seen as something that can reinforce energy security.”

Recent global policymaking reflects this notion. China’s newest five-year plan now accounts for the arrival of peak oil, while 25 countries have adopted electrification policies this year alone. And at the ongoing COP31 United Nations climate conference, the central pledge will be for the world to achieve 35 percent electrification by 2035 – a goal which cheap Chinese components and the war in Iran have suddenly put within “striking distance.”

analysis.tldr: Global oil prices jumping due to war are pushing China to use much less oil and coal, which could eventually lower global demand for fossil fuels and make green energy technologies even cheaper for importing countries like India.
the_story: The war in Iran is causing an enduring upset in global oil and gas markets, leading to skyrocketing energy prices worldwide.
China's carbon dioxide emissions saw their biggest fall since the COVID pandemic in the third quarter of this year, dropping 3.1 percent between July and September.
China's oil consumption fell by 4 percent year-on-year as consumers ditched conventional gas-burning engines for electric vehicles to escape high oil prices.
China's coal emissions fell by 3 percent year-on-year due to a massive buildout of renewable energy resources like wind, solar, and nuclear.
Developing economies like Pakistan, Brazil, Chile, and others are rapidly adopting cheap Chinese solar panels and batteries to secure affordable energy and avoid market volatility.
analysis.what_happened: The ongoing war in Iran has disrupted global energy supplies and caused oil prices to skyrocket. Because conventional fuel has become so expensive, consumers in China rushed to buy electric vehicles, and the country's massive investments in wind and solar power finally caused its oil and coal consumption to drop significantly.
analysis.analogy: It is like a family reacting to a sudden spike in petrol prices by finally buying a electric scooter and putting solar panels on the roof to stop paying unpredictable fuel bills.
why_it_matters_india: Middle-East conflict disrupts global oil supplies, driving up international crude prices.
Major oil consumers like China react by cutting down on oil usage and accelerating green energy adoption.
Increased global manufacturing of cheap solar panels and batteries by China drives down equipment prices worldwide.
India, which imports most of its energy, benefits from cheaper renewable technology imports to secure its own energy independence.

impacts.rationale: War in Iran creates global oil supply concerns, pushing pump prices higher—bad for household budgets in India.

impacts.target: India's inflation rate (the rate at which everyday prices rise)
impacts.rationale: Costlier imported energy makes transport and manufacturing more expensive, raising the cost of living for regular people.
Higher oil import bills mean India needs more US dollars, which can weaken the local currency and make foreign goods pricier.

watch_next: Whether global oil prices remain high or stabilize following the disruptions from Iran
The pace at which solar panel and battery manufacturing costs continue to drop globally
analysis.caveats: The article focuses primarily on China's domestic shifts and global green adoption; if the war in Iran escalates further, oil price spikes could overwhelm the downward pressure from reduced Chinese demand.

items.title: RBI may hike interest rates by 75 basis points by Q2 of next year: Goldman Sachs
items.summary: The Reserve Bank of India is projected to increase interest rates by 75 basis points by the second quarter of 2027. Analysts predict that headline inflation will remain above 6 percent into early 2027 before gradually decreasing. Despite the monetary tightening, India's GDP growth is expected to moderate to 7.2 percent in 2027. Strong domestic demand and an emerging investment cycle are likely to sustain economic activity.

events.article_text:
The Reserve Bank of India is projected to increase interest rates by 75 basis points by the second quarter of 2027. Despite the monetary tightening, India's GDP growth is expected to moderate to 7.2 percent in 2027. Strong domestic demand and an emerging investment cycle are likely to sustain economic activity.

analysis.tldr: If the Reserve Bank makes borrowing costlier to fight high prices, ordinary people will likely face higher interest rates on their home and car loans.
the_story: Goldman Sachs projects the Reserve Bank of India (RBI, India's central bank) will increase interest rates by 75 basis points (0.75 percentage points) by the second quarter of 2027.
Analysts predict headline inflation (the overall cost of living based on a basket of common goods) will stay above 6 percent until early 2027 before slowly coming down.
Even with these interest rate hikes, India's GDP growth (Gross Domestic Product, the total value of goods and services produced) is expected to slow down to 7.2 percent in 2027.
Strong local demand and a pick-up in business investments are expected to keep the economy moving forward despite the tighter monetary policy (RBI actions to slow down borrowing and spending).
analysis.what_happened: Goldman Sachs released a forecast stating that the Reserve Bank of India will likely raise interest rates by 0.75 percentage points by mid-2027. This is expected because inflation (rising prices) is predicted to stay stubbornly above 6 percent until early 2027, forcing the central bank to make borrowing more expensive to cool down price rises.
analysis.analogy: It is like a doctor prescribing a bitter medicine (higher interest rates) to bring a high fever (inflation) down, which slows the patient (the economy) down a bit in the process.
why_it_matters_india: RBI expects inflation to stay above 6 percent through early 2027, meaning everyday goods remain costly.
To fight this, the RBI is projected to hike interest rates by 75 basis points by Q2 of 2027.
When the central bank hikes rates, commercial banks make loans more expensive for ordinary citizens and businesses.
This cooling effect is expected to moderate India's economic growth rate to 7.2 percent in 2027.

impacts.target: Home and car loan EMIs (Equated Monthly Installments, your fixed monthly loan payments)
impacts.rationale: Higher RBI interest rates mean banks raise their lending rates, making monthly loan payments more expensive for borrowers — generally bad for people with active loans.
Raising interest rates slows down spending, which helps bring rising prices down over time — good for household budgets in the long run.

impacts.target: Nifty 50 (India's main stock index containing top 50 companies)
impacts.rationale: Higher borrowing costs can squeeze company profits and slow economic growth, which sometimes causes temporary caution in the stock market — can be stressful for investors.

watch_next: Official inflation data releases from the government to see if prices are staying above 6 percent
Future statements from the Reserve Bank of India regarding their actual interest rate decisions
analysis.caveats: This report is a financial analyst forecast for 2027, and actual RBI actions could change depending on how global commodity prices and domestic weather patterns affect inflation.

analysis.what_happened: Indian government bonds gained value early on because international investors bought them up. This happened while global factors like US borrowing costs stabilized and crude oil prices held steady. At the same time, traders are getting ready for the Reserve Bank of India to potentially raise interest rates in December.
analysis.analogy: It is like a popular neighborhood park bench where demand fluctuates; when more people from out of town decide to sit there, the current spots become more valued, but everyone keeps a nervous eye on how loud the neighbors get next door.
why_it_matters_india: International investors buy Indian government bonds -> demand for these bonds goes up -> bond prices rise.
Global factors like crude oil prices and US Treasury yields move -> these shifts dictate how foreign money flows in and out of India.
Markets start expecting a possible interest rate hike by the Reserve Bank of India in December -> lenders and borrowers prepare for tighter financial conditions.
Bond yields fluctuate slightly -> affects the cost for the government and major banks to borrow money.

Any official announcements or signals from the Reserve Bank of India regarding the anticipated December meeting

events.headline: Shrinkflation and the constraints of monetary tightening

items.title: Shrinkflation and the constraints of monetary tightening
items.summary: The RBI’s 25-basis-point repo rate hike is aimed at cost-push inflation. How producers respond to rising prices determines whether it works.

events.article_text:
Published : Nov 19, 2026 14:16 IST - 5 MINS READ

A pedestrian walks past the entrance of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) headquarters in Mumbai on October 7, 2026. India's central bank hiked interest rates for the first time in more than three years on October 7, as the Middle East conflict stokes inflation in Asia's third-largest economy and batters a weakened rupee. | Photo Credit: PUNIT PARANJPE/AFP

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) raised the policy repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 per cent on October 7, 2026, its first increase since February 2023. The aim is to bring down cost-push inflation, driven by higher energy prices after the conflict in West Asia.

According to conventional economic theory, a central bank can reduce the demand for credit by raising interest rates, which slows the rise in prices. Cost-push inflation complicates this, because higher rates reduce both corporate and consumer demand.

The cost is not only higher equated monthly instalments (EMIs). Jobs are also lost or never created.

Policymakers therefore need to know how producers react to inflation. The market and the state respond differently, and each can learn from the other.

This article looks at three market responses to inflation and how public policy responds to each. They are shrinkflation, skimpflation, and expandingstatic, the article’s term for offering more of a product at an unchanged price.

Shrinkflation is a hidden price increase: manufacturers reduce a product’s weight, size, or quantity and keep the price the same. In 2022, Hindustan Unilever’s Rs.10 Vim bar went from 155 g to 135 g, and a Haldiram’s aloo bhujia pack at the same price went from 55 g to 42 g.

Consumers pay the same for less and must buy more often. Their purchasing power falls, and the extra spending adds to inflation.

The evidence on scale is mixed. In 2017, the UK’s Office for National Statistics found that shrinking packs had no effect on overall inflation, though they raised the prices of chocolates and sweets.

Shrinkflation does not stop price increases. It hides them, and inflation stays high long after the original causes have gone.

Once prices settle at a higher level, they stay there. Producers then move to expandingstatic: they increase a product’s quantity or size, or bundle accessories with it, at prevailing prices.

Customers get more for the same money and buy less often, so spending falls. With prices high enough to reward output, the law of supply applies: rising prices encourage rising production.

Skimpflation is the practice of lowering the quality of a product or service while keeping the price unchanged. Producers use cheaper ingredients, cut staff, cut service features, or offer fewer amenities.

In a wealthy society, where consumers are sensitive to quality, poor products and services discourage repeat purchases. In a poor society, skimpflation persists and has effects similar to those of shrinkflation.

Laws and regulation limit the practice, as does business ethics. How far skimpflation succeeds depends on the relationship between political economy and society, and that relationship limits how long the market can use it.

When a central bank raises the repo rate during shrinkflation, it asks consumers to spend less, although they already have to buy more often to get the same quantity. Policy and social reality conflict.

Households facing shrinkflation and higher borrowing costs spend less on industrial goods and more on essentials, and their standard of living falls. Fiscal policy can respond with tax cuts, higher public spending, or both, to raise demand for industrial goods, production, and living standards.

Manufacturers, however, have little reason to raise production during shrinkflation. They have raised effective prices, sell fewer industrial goods, and earn higher mark-ups.

Monetary tightening therefore fails to bring inflation down during shrinkflation. It also adds to household distress and makes fiscal policy less effective.

Expandingstatic works differently. It stabilises prices at a higher level, and with more product on offer at the same price, spending falls.

Stable prices allow the central bank to cut the repo rate, which raises industrial output. Producers can also use the reserve capacity they built up from the mark-ups they earned during shrinkflation.

At this stage the government can raise public spending and the central bank can ease monetary policy, and producers are likely to increase output. A larger state can also crowd in private producers through positive externalities, although many economists warn that heavy government borrowing can crowd out private investment by raising interest rates.

These conditions encourage investment in alternative production methods and goods that reduce the effects of cost-push inflation. Rising fuel prices, for instance, have contributed to higher manufacture and sale of electric vehicles.

Because law and business ethics keep skimpflation in check, it does not bring the market into conflict with state policy. Shrinkflation does.

During shrinkflation, consumers must spend more while the central bank wants them to spend less, and producers cut quantity while fiscal policy tries to raise consumption. Producers, consumers, and public policy work at cross-purposes.

Public policy is more likely to succeed during expandingstatic, when producers and policymakers both want more output. Rising output brings more jobs, in line with the Phillips curve, which posits a short-run trade-off between inflation and unemployment.

Whether the RBI’s October hike works depends on which of the two applies. If producers keep shrinking packs, tightening alone will not bring down cost-push inflation, and public policy must work to reduce shrinkflation and speed up expandingstatic.

Ajay Kumar Mishra teaches Economics at Lalit Narayan Mithila University, Darbhanga, Bihar. He has obtained his PhD from the Centre for South Asian Studies, JNU, New Delhi.

analysis.tldr: The Reserve Bank of India raised interest rates to fight inflation, but hidden price tricks by companies mean your household budget will feel extra squeezed with costlier loans and stealthy price hikes.
the_story: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) raised its policy repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 per cent on October 7, 2026, marking its first increase since February 2023.
The rate hike aims to combat cost-push inflation driven by higher energy prices stemming from the conflict in West Asia.

Companies use shrinkflation to hide price hikes by reducing a product's size or weight while keeping the price the same; examples include Hindustan Unilever's Vim bar dropping from 155g to 135g in 2022, and Haldiram's aloo bhujia pack shrinking from 55g to 42g.
Skimpflation involves lowering product quality or cutting staff and services while maintaining prices, which persists longer in poorer societies.
When a central bank raises borrowing costs while households face shrinkflation, people are forced to spend more on essentials, making monetary tightening less effective at lowering inflation.
analysis.what_happened: The Reserve Bank of India raised its key borrowing rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 per cent on October 7, 2026, to cool down inflation caused by surging energy prices from the West Asia conflict. However, because companies are practicing shrinkflation—giving you less product for the same price—households are already forced to spend more often, putting consumers and the central bank's goals at odds.
analysis.analogy: It is like a grocery shop owner quietly cutting your bag of rice from 10 kilos to 8 kilos while still charging you for 10, just as your bank raises your home loan EMI to stop you from spending.
why_it_matters_india: The RBI raises the repo rate (the interest rate the central bank charges commercial banks to borrow money) to 5.50%.
Commercial banks pass these higher costs down, making equated monthly instalments (EMIs) for home, auto, and personal loans more expensive.
At the same time, companies practice shrinkflation (reducing package sizes for the same price) because of higher energy costs.
Households must spend more money on everyday necessities more frequently, squeezing their budgets even further alongside higher loan payments.

impacts.target: Cost of loans (home, auto, and personal loan EMIs)
impacts.rationale: higher repo rates mean banks charge borrowers more, which is generally bad for ordinary people carrying debt.
hidden price increases like shrinkflation keep effective inflation high long after the original energy shocks settle, which hurts consumer purchasing power.

impacts.target: Electric vehicles and alternative energy products
impacts.rationale: rising fuel prices push manufacturers and consumers toward alternative products like electric vehicles, which can eventually help lower energy dependence.

watch_next: Whether companies continue to shrink package sizes or shift toward expandingstatic (offering more product at steady prices)
Future policy announcements from the Reserve Bank of India regarding further interest rate adjustments
analysis.caveats: The success of the RBI's rate hike depends heavily on how manufacturers respond and whether fiscal policy steps in with tax cuts or public spending to support living standards.

events.headline: DDG Nordquist: Global trade is adapting, not retreating

items.title: DDG Nordquist: Global trade is adapting, not retreating
items.summary: Global trade has demonstrated remarkable resilience despite geopolitical tensions, supply chain disruptions and trade restrictions, with businesses adapting through diversification and new trading partnerships, Deputy Director-General DJ Nordquist said at the 16th Asian Logistics, Maritime and Aviation Conference in Hong Kong, China, on 16 November. Highlighting stronger-than-expected trade growth and the continued importance of WTO rules, she called for more resilient global supply chains, deeper international cooperation and reforms to ensure the multilateral trading system remains fit for t

events.article_text:
Excellencies, distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen,

It is a real pleasure to be here in Hong Kong, and I would like to begin by thanking our hosts for their kind invitation and warm welcome.

I looked up a bit of history and was very interested to learn that Hong Kong boasts the most skyscrapers in the world, but you still have set aside 40% of your land area for parks and nature reserves. I also learned that Hong Kong translates to "fragrant harbor," making you one of the only cities named after a smell - which was actually trade in incense! Maybe later today I will even spot some of your famous pink dolphins!

It is actually my first time back in Hong Kong in almost 30 years, which coincidentally is also when WTO came into being. Much has changed over those three decades, both here and in the world around us.

But one thing that has certainly not changed is Hong Kong's remarkable energy, economic dynamism, and its enduring role as a gateway connecting businesses and markets across the world.

I can think of few places more fitting than Hong Kong to discuss the future of global supply chains and international trade. Hong Kong's success as an international trading and logistics hub - your trade to GDP ratio is almost 400 per cent!!! -- is a powerful illustration of how trade can drive growth, create opportunities, and connect economies across borders - objectives that also lie at the very heart of the WTO's mission.

On a side note, I was thinking about the phrase "supply chains" because I feel like it wasn't really a buzzword until fairly recently - it seems to have become popular in the 1990s, just as WTO was being formed. It's actually been around for over a century - it was first used in 1905, and catalogued in the Merriam-Webster dictionary almost a half century later in 1948, just about when the WTO's predecessor, the GATT, as established. So there are some interesting connections in the verbiage and the history of the global trading system under GATT and WTO!

Over the past 3 decades, we have witnessed an extraordinary transformation of global trade: the rise of global value chains, the digital revolution, and changes in economic power. At the same time, we've seen growing geopolitical tensions. Governments are increasingly concerned about economic and national security, and strategic over-dependencies, while businesses are reacting by reassessing their supply chains, which includes by diversifying suppliers and other ways to provide greater certainty in a today's environment.

Yet, despite these pressures, global trade has demonstrated remarkable resilience. I am here to be an optimist!

In 2025, world merchandise trade volumes grew by 4.6 per cent, significantly exceeding earlier expectations -- our economists had initially projected negative growth.

How did it happen? Strong demand for AI-related goods and the ability of businesses to adapt to changing trade conditions.

This resilience has continued this year. According to the WTO's latest Global Trade Outlook, published in October, world merchandise trade volumes are expected to grow by 3.9% in 2026 (more than double the March forecast) and 4.1% in 2027. Meanwhile commercial services trade is expected to grow of 3.3% in 2026 and 6.4% in 2027.

Notably, merchandise trade growth has been outpacing global GDP growth quite significantly for the second year in a row, reversing the trend seen for much of the period since the global financial crisis which was characterized by near parity between trade growth and GDP growth. So we seem to be reverting to the norms of the pre-2008 period, when international trade typically expanded much faster than global economic output.

And this has all happened in spite of the disruptions to energy markets, transport routes, and supply chains. It demonstrates the adaptability of global trade networks and the interconnectedness of the global economy.

So I'd say global trade is not disappearing in the face of uncertainty - it is adapting and evolving.

At the same time, the trade policy environment continues to face challenges.

Our latest WTO Trade Monitoring Report, issued just a few weeks ago, shows that trade policy activity has intensified significantly. I probably don't need to tell you that - you live it every day.

I am going to start with the good news. Our economists found that in the first half of 2026, WTO members introduced 466 trade-facilitating measures, which is more than during all of 2025. Trade facilitation was focused in response to the Hormuz situation -- which is a positive - and different than what we saw in Covid and the Russia/Ukraine war.

On the other hand, in the first six months of 2026 alone, WTO Members and Observers introduced also 333 new restrictive and other non-facilitating trade measures, exceeding the 300 recorded during all of 2025.

The cumulative stock of such import-related measures introduced since 2009 and still in force today is affecting over 21 per cent of world imports, worth some $5.4 trillion.

But if you take a holistic look at the trading system, as our economists have, 72 per cent of global goods trade continues to take place on WTO's most-favoured-nation terms (meaning WTO's standard, non-discriminatory tariff rules, rather than under special preferential trade arrangements).

These findings highlight both the growing pressures on global trade and the enduring importance of WTO rules as an anchor of stability, predictability, and cooperation.

Recent economic shocks have exposed the risks associated with excessive dependence on a limited number of suppliers or markets. Businesses learned that lesson in real time. But resilience should not be confused with isolation or autarky - as my earlier numbers show, trade is alive and well.

The partners may have changed, but the dance continues. I am not sure whether the dance is the Tai Hang Fire dance, a tango, or a ballet. But the music, and movement to it, is still going strong.

WTO research

analysis.tldr: Global trade is growing faster than expected despite tensions, which helps Indian exporters find steady international demand.
the_story: World merchandise trade volumes grew by 4.6 per cent in 2025, beating earlier negative expectations due to strong demand for AI-related goods and business adaptability.
The WTO's Global Trade Outlook expects world merchandise trade volumes to grow by 3.9% in 2026 and 4.1% in 2027, with commercial services trade growing 3.3% in 2026 and 6.4% in 2027.
In the first half of 2026, WTO members introduced 466 trade-facilitating measures (responding to the Hormuz situation) and 333 new restrictive trade measures.
Currently, 72 per cent of global goods trade still happens on WTO's standard, non-discriminatory tariff rules (most-favoured-nation terms).
analysis.what_happened: A top World Trade Organization official, DDG Nordquist, stated in a speech in Hong Kong that global trade is adapting rather than retreating, driven by strong demand for artificial intelligence goods and flexible supply chains. Despite rising geopolitical tensions and new trade restrictions, global trade volumes are growing faster than overall global economic output.
analysis.analogy: It is like a bustling local market where, even if a few shop owners put up temporary fences, the shoppers simply find new pathways to buy and sell goods, keeping the overall bazaar busier than ever.
why_it_matters_india: Global trade volumes grow -> International demand for goods and services increases -> Indian tech and merchandise exporters receive more orders -> Boosts revenues for Indian export-oriented companies.

Governments introduce trade-facilitating measures -> Supply chain bottlenecks ease -> Import and export processes become smoother for Indian logistics and manufacturing firms -> Lowers operational friction.

Geopolitical tensions and strategic over-dependencies cause businesses to diversify suppliers -> Global companies look beyond traditional hubs like China (China Plus One strategy) -> India attracts more global manufacturing investments and supply chain contracts.

impacts.rationale: Stronger global trade and tech demand support earnings for India's major export and IT firms, which is generally good for broader market sentiment.
Robust global commercial services trade growth points to healthy tech spending from overseas clients, which is good for revenues of Indian IT majors.

watch_next: Updates on the implementation of trade-facilitating measures responding to the Hormuz situation
Future revisions to WTO global trade volume forecasts for 2026 and 2027
analysis.caveats: While overall trade is proving resilient, an escalation in new restrictive trade measures (which already reached 333 in the first half of 2026) could disrupt specific supply routes and dampen growth.

events.article_text:
For this edition of The Atlantic Brief, the Royal United Services Institute and War on the Rocks present a dialogue on the future of trans-Atlantic defense cooperation following the U.S. midterm elections. Participating experts from the United Kingdom, continental Europe, and the United States bring decades of first-hand experience in the armed forces, diplomacy, and foreign policy.

The panel will explore what the midterms mean for U.S. force posture, NATO, and support for Ukraine. It will also cover European investment in defense capabilities, the questions of strained supply chains, and whether NATO or the European Union should lead in countering…

analysis.tldr: A high-level policy dialogue on Western defense cooperation after U.S. elections has no direct, immediate effect on your everyday finances, loans, or the prices you pay.
the_story: The Royal United Services Institute and War on the Rocks hosted a dialogue on trans-Atlantic defense cooperation after U.S. midterm elections.
Experts from the United Kingdom, continental Europe, and the United States participated, drawing on backgrounds in the armed forces, diplomacy, and foreign policy.

The panel discussion explored topics including U.S. military presence, NATO (North Atlantic Treaty Organization, a military alliance of North American and European countries), and ongoing support for Ukraine.
The conversation also covered European defense spending, strained supply chains, and whether NATO or the European Union should lead counter-efforts.
analysis.what_happened: Experts from the U.S., U.K., and Europe met to discuss how political shifts from U.S. midterm elections will impact military alliances, support for Ukraine, and European defense spending. Because the article only describes a panel discussion and cuts off before any conclusions or policy decisions are announced, no actual laws or spending plans changed.
analysis.analogy: It is like a group of retired managers meeting to debate how a company's new board of directors might change its security budget, but without making any actual business decisions yet.
why_it_matters_india: Experts discuss Western military strategy and funding in Europe and the U.S.
This shapes long-term global defense policies and international weapon supply chains.
Since India mostly buys defense equipment independently and maintains a non-aligned foreign policy, these regional Western debates do not directly shift Indian domestic markets.
Therefore, the domestic impact on Indian inflation, the rupee (each rupee buys fewer dollars), and everyday borrowing costs remains negligible.

impacts.rationale: Global geopolitical debates rarely shift Indian stock markets directly unless they involve immediate trade or oil supply shocks.
A discussion on Western defense policy does not alter global currency flows or the value of the rupee.
Without changes to global oil supplies or trade tariffs, local prices for food and fuel remain unaffected.

watch_next: Actual policy announcements or defense budget changes passed by the U.S. government or European nations
Any shifts in global defense manufacturing contracts that might involve Indian aerospace or defense companies
analysis.caveats: The source text is incomplete and only describes a panel discussion without reporting any final policy decisions or concrete outcomes.

events.headline: The world struggles to pay for the growing human cost of climate change

items.title: The world struggles to pay for the growing human cost of climate change
items.summary: In 2022, floodwater engulfed the farm and home of Abdul Khalique Laghari, a farmer from Pakistan’s Sindh province. The water rose six to eight feet in some places. The crops were destroyed, houses were inundated and the land was left damaged. Four years later, farmers in the region are still struggling to cultivate it. “Our […]

events.article_text:
If you liked this story, share it with other people.

In 2022, floodwater engulfed the farm and home of Abdul Khalique Laghari, a farmer from Pakistan’s Sindh province. The water rose six to eight feet in some places. The crops were destroyed, houses were inundated and the land was left damaged. Four years later, farmers in the region are still struggling to cultivate it. “Our farms were underwater. The water entered our houses. Everything was destroyed,” Laghari said. He and more than 30 other farmers from Sindh are now seeking compensation for their losses.

Their experience shows how climate damage reaches far beyond the moment a disaster strikes. A farmer loses not just a crop, but the income needed to feed a family and pay off debt. A coastal household may find its drinking water contaminated by salt. A fishing community may see its catch decline as the sea changes. An island community may face the loss of the land on which its history and identity are rooted.

These are the human costs of climate change, increasingly recognised in international negotiations as loss and damage. They include the destruction caused by floods, storms and heatwaves, but also the slower damage from rising seas, coastal erosion and saltwater intrusion. Some losses can be repaired with money. Others are irreversible.

The scale of the problem is growing. The World Meteorological Organization’s climate update, released as the annual UN climate summit in Türkiye’s Antalya opened, says the past 12 years are set to be the warmest on record. Sea levels and ocean heat have also reached record highs. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, a body of climate scientists and experts, has warned that human-induced climate change is already causing widespread losses and damage to people and nature.

Yet the international response remains far behind the needs of those affected. That gap is a central challenge for nearly 200 countries meeting in Antalya.

The creation of the Fund for responding to Loss and Damage in 2022 was a breakthrough. Developing countries had spent decades demanding financial support for damage that could no longer be prevented through reducing emissions or avoided through adaptation. The fund was meant to help vulnerable countries deal with the destruction of homes, infrastructure, livelihoods and ecosystems.

But its resources are nowhere near the demand. The fund received 176 requests from 119 countries in its first funding round, seeking a total of $2.8 billion. It had set aside only $342 million. The fund’s secretariat is reviewing the requests, with an initial package due before its board in December.

Nor has all the money pledged by governments reached the fund. A UN climate negotiations document records $822.71 million in pledges, of which only $485.77 million had been received by July 31. The fund’s first replenishment process is due to begin in 2027. A draft decision before the Antalya summit calls for new, substantial and predictable grants from developed countries. But the question is whether governments will match these promises with money.

Harjeet Singh, global convenor of the Fill the Fund campaign and founding director of the Satat Sampada Climate Foundation, described the fund as “a lifeboat with no oars.” A few hundred million dollars in voluntary pledges cannot meet the scale of the destruction, he said. Vulnerable countries need grants on a much larger scale, not loans that deepen their debt.

Nepal illustrates the gulf between the money available and the cost of recovery. The August floods due to a glacier collapse in the Bhote Koshi valley killed more than 1,400 people and left thousands missing. The World Bank estimates that recovery and reconstruction will cost about $4.8 billion. The loss and damage fund has provisionally set aside just $21.6 million for Nepal. The allocation is a welcome step, but it is not yet money disbursed and represents only a tiny fraction of the country’s needs.

“I come here from a nation still in grief,” Nepal’s foreign minister Shisir Khanal told the summit. “This is the time to put sympathy into the system, and promises into action.”

The problem is not only the size of the fund. Countries must prepare proposals and wait for approvals before money can be released. That takes time, while families need shelter, farmers need to restore their land and communities need basic services. For people already struggling to recover, delays can mean another lost season or another year without a secure home.

The UN Climate Change’s loss and damage team was approached for comment, but had not responded by the time of publication.

The urgency is particularly clear in South Asia. Pakistan’s farmers are still dealing with the aftermath of the 2022 floods. Nepal is facing the enormous task of rebuilding after the recent disaster. In coastal Bangladesh, saltwater intrusion, storm surges and erosion are damaging farmland, freshwater supplies and livelihoods. A 2026 study in coastal Shyamnagar, a coastal area of Bangladesh found that the damage also affects health, cultural practices and social ties.

India faces similar pressures along its coast, including in the Sundarbans, where erosion and saltwater intrusion threaten homes and livelihoods. For families dependent on farming and fishing, the damage is not a single event but a steady erosion of their ability to make a living. Better records of such losses are essential, but documenting the damage will not compensate a family whose land has turned saline or whose home has been washed away.

On Pari Island, north of Jakarta in Indonesia, around 4,000 people live on just over 41 hectares. Residents have faced tidal flooding since the early 2000s. Large-scale flooding worsened from 2019 and reached its worst point in 2021. Rising seas, stronger waves, warmer seawater and changing fishing patterns threaten their homes and livelihoods.

Four residents have taken a case against cement producer Holcim in Switze

analysis.tldr: Global climate disaster relief funds are falling drastically short of what developing nations need, which will force governments like India to spend more of their own taxpayer money on domestic climate disaster recovery.
the_story: In 2022, severe floods destroyed the farm and home of Abdul Khalique Laghari in Pakistan's Sindh province, and four years later, farmers in the region are still struggling to cultivate their damaged land.

A specialized international 'Fund for responding to Loss and Damage' created in 2022 received 176 requests totaling $2.8 billion from 119 countries in its first funding round, but had only set aside $342 million.
Although governments pledged $822.71 million in total, only $485.77 million actually reached the fund by July 31, leading campaigners to describe the fund as a lifeboat with no oars.

Nepal faced a massive disaster when August floods from a glacier collapse in the Bhote Koshi valley killed over 1,400 people, with the World Bank estimating recovery costs at $4.8 billion while the loss and damage fund provisionally set aside just $21.6 million.
South Asian nations like India face similar pressures along vulnerable coastlines including the Sundarbans, where coastal erosion and saltwater intrusion threaten homes, farmland, and livelihoods.
analysis.what_happened: International bodies and nearly 200 countries meeting at a UN climate summit in Antalya are grappling with a massive shortfall in money available to help vulnerable nations deal with climate disasters. The cause is a massive gap between voluntary financial promises made by wealthy nations and the actual destruction caused by record-breaking global temperatures, rising seas, and severe weather.
analysis.analogy: It is like a neighborhood setting up a small community disaster jar with loose change, when several houses have just completely burned down and require millions to rebuild.
why_it_matters_india: International climate aid falls far short of actual disaster costs in South Asia, including India's vulnerable coastlines like the Sundarbans.
Because global funds cannot cover local climate destruction, the Indian government must rely more heavily on its own domestic budgets to rebuild infrastructure and support affected farmers.
Higher domestic spending on disaster recovery can strain government finances, pushing up the amount the government needs to borrow.
Increased government borrowing can raise domestic interest rates and stoke inflation if food production is hit repeatedly by extreme weather events.

impacts.target: 10-year bond yield (interest India pays to borrow)
impacts.rationale: If the government has to spend more of its own money on climate disaster relief and reconstruction without international help, it may borrow more, pushing up bond yields — which generally makes loans costlier for regular people.
Frequent floods, storms, and saltwater damage destroy crops and push up food prices, which is bad for household budgets.

watch_next: Updates on how much wealthy countries actually disburse to the Loss and Damage fund at future UN climate summits
Announcements from Indian state governments regarding disaster relief budgets for coastal regions like the Sundarbans
analysis.caveats: This text cuts off mid-sentence, but the core reporting on global climate funding shortfalls and South Asian vulnerabilities is fully established.

events.article_text:
An official website of the United States Government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock () or https:// means you've safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

The Federal Reserve Board on Thursday announced pricing, effective January 1, 2027, for payment services the Federal Reserve Banks provide to banks and credit unions, such as the clearing of checks, automated clearing house (ACH) transactions, instant payments, and wholesale payment and settlement services.

By law, the Federal Reserve must establish fees to recover the costs, including imputed costs, of providing payment services over the long run. The Federal Reserve expects to recover 101.5 percent of actual and imputed expenses in 2027, including the return on equity that would have been earned if a private-sector firm provided the services. Overall, price changes for 2027 will result in an estimated 1.4 percent average price increase for established, mature services.

In addition, the Federal Reserve Banks announced changes to streamline and adjust their check services. As described in the request for information on check services issued last year, the volume of checks processed by the Federal Reserve Banks is declining, but checks remain an important payment instrument for many consumers and businesses. The changes were informed by public feedback and ensure that the Federal Reserve Banks continue to provide check services efficiently. The adjustments include optimizing check processing windows during low-volume periods, increasing fees that banks and credit unions pay to process checks, and other operational updates. These changes do not impact consumers' and businesses' ability to pay with or receive checks and only impact how banks and credit unions process checks with Federal Reserve Banks.

The entire 2027 fee schedule for all of the Federal Reserve's payment services is published on FRBservices.org®. Additional information on the Federal Reserve's payments services, including service usage statistics, is available on the Board's website.

For media inquiries, please email [email protected] or call 202-452-2955.â¯â¯

analysis.tldr: Changes to fees and check processing by the US central bank will have virtually no direct impact on your everyday finances, loans, or the Indian stock market.
the_story: The US Federal Reserve Board announced new pricing for payment services that Federal Reserve Banks provide to banks and credit unions, effective January 1, 2027.
These services include clearing checks, automated clearing house transactions, instant payments, and wholesale payment and settlement services.
The Federal Reserve expects to recover 101.5 percent of its costs for these services in 2027, resulting in an estimated 1.4 percent average price increase for mature services.
Check services are being streamlined because processing volumes are declining, which includes optimizing processing windows and raising fees for banks and credit unions.
analysis.what_happened: The US central bank announced upcoming fee changes and operational adjustments for the payment and check-processing services it provides to American commercial banks and credit unions, set to take effect on January 1, 2027. This decision is driven by a legal requirement to recover its operating costs over the long run as check volumes decline.
analysis.analogy: It is like a central printing press for a private club raising the membership fees it charges local club branches for handling paperwork, which only affects the internal members of that specific club.
why_it_matters_india: The announcement concerns domestic banking operations inside the United States.
There are no direct connections to Indian payment systems, retail banking, or Indian monetary policy.
Consequently, it does not trigger any financial ripples that affect Indian inflation, currency exchange rates, or local stock prices.

impacts.rationale: Internal US banking administrative fee updates do not alter the broader exchange rate between the two currencies.
This regulatory update for US financial institutions has no bearing on the earnings or valuations of Indian companies.

watch_next: Broader US interest rate decisions by the Federal Open Market Committee
Global economic data releases affecting international markets
analysis.caveats: This update is strictly procedural and administrative for the US financial system, carrying no domestic ripple effects for India.

events.headline: This smell startup says its AI nose is as good as a human’s

items.title: This smell startup says its AI nose is as good as a human’s
items.summary: In a lab near Newark Airport in New Jersey, a team of around 30 experienced human sniffers are slowly working their way through every odor on Earth. Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with a chemical analysis to create a rich set of training data for what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation…

events.article_text:
In a lab near Newark Airport in New Jersey, a team of around 30 experienced human sniffers are slowly working their way through every odor on Earth. Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with a chemical analysis to create a rich set of training data for what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation model for smell. The company’s goal, says founder Alex Wiltschko, is “to give computers a sense of smell.”

“Scent molecules are really the only language most species on this planet can speak,” he says. “Most species can’t communicate with sound or visually, so it truly is Earth’s original language. And it’s incredibly powerful for us, from a memory and an emotional standpoint. You can smell something once and remember it for the rest of your life. You can smell something on the street and be pulled back to high school.”

In the last few months, Wiltschko claims, Osmo’s model has achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence.” The company’s definition of this is that the model is about as good as the average person at detecting and discriminating between smells, and about as good as a junior perfume designer at creating them. It says its technology is already being used in the fragrance industry to help brands design and manufacture new scents. Last month, the company says, Osmo’s AI model outperformed in-house perfumers at one of the world’s largest consumer goods companies. Wiltschko believes it could be deployed eventually for threat detection at airports, for example, or diagnosing diseases.

Wiltschko spun the startup out of his work at Google Brain, the search giant’s former AI research lab, in 2023, and he is running the same playbook as AI startups in other domains: Throw a lot of data at difficult problems, and see what happens. The challenge with scent, Wiltschko says, is that there was a dearth of good data. Before Osmo, there were fewer than 200,000 human descriptions of smells in existing databases, by his count. Plus, the chemical sensor devices needed to collect data are expensive, and the fragrance industry is secretive about its work on olfactory science.

A lot of the company’s work has been in creating its own dataset of more than 10 million human labels and 800 million “scent tokens,” which describe the exact molecules and concentrations that go into creating specific odors. Osmo uses spectrometers and other chemical sensors, running around the clock, to break down the molecular makeup of everything from fruit and flowers to pantry staples and organs. A team of around 70 trained data labelers in the US and overseas spend their days sniffing things and writing down what they smell like, using a standardized fragrance vocabulary.

Mapping out scents in this way is throwing out some unlikely parallels. In the same way that changing the order of words can drastically influence the meaning of a sentence, rearranging scent molecules in different proportions can drastically alter the smells humans perceive. “The scent tokens that define the smell of a newborn baby have massive overlap with the scent tokens in a fresh plate of cooked spaghetti,” Wiltschko says. (Specifically Barilla brand spaghetti, he says, which perhaps raises some questions for the people at the pasta factory.)

The company also creates its own scents, using a smell-printing robot the size of a school bus that mixes ingredients according to precise formulas to make samples for Osmo’s own research and fragrances for paying customers. It can design and print scents to order based on a ChatGPT-style prompt. Wiltschko flipped open his laptop to show me how the AI model worked. He opened a text box on screen, and I asked him to generate a fragrance that smelled like a Portuguese custard tart (we were in Lisbon for Web Summit), aimed at 18- to 23-year-old men. The system spent a few minutes cogitating, then generated three options for potential scent profiles that matched the brief (creamy, coconutty, fruity) and the molecules needed to create them. If I’d continued with the ordering process, my signature L’Eau de Custard would have been ready about a week later.

Osmo’s technology has already been used to create retail fragrances, including for giants like Procter & Gamble. The Gates Foundation, which invested $5 million when Osmo launched, later gave the company a $3.5 million grant to assess molecules that repel disease-carrying insects, and Osmo identified eight substances that were more repellent than DEET. Osmo has also worked with StockX, the online clothing marketplace, on using smell to spot counterfeit sneakers by detecting differences in the chemical composition of the materials used in the shoes.

But not everyone is convinced by the technology or the company’s big claims. Avery Gilbert, a smell scientist and author of What the Nose Knows, has been sharply critical of Osmo on his Substack, arguing that some of its marketing claims are undocumented, and that its patent filings still rely on human sensory panels and perfumers, rather than AI. “This heavy reliance on human sensory judgments seems odd for a company premised on super-cool AI,” he wrote in March. A representative for Osmo did not respond in time for publication.

Michael Schmuker, a former professor of neural computation at the University of Hertfordshire who has previously consulted for Osmo, says the company’s technology is an achievement. With colleagues, he created an open-source, reverse-engineered version of Osmo’s 2023 model, but it lacks the reams of data the company has collected since.

But even with all this smell data, Osmo may be missing some of the factors that make human olfaction unique, Schmuker says. “Smell is super complex. Context is very important for smell. The same molecule may evoke a different association depending on context,” he says. “[The smell of] a French cheese like Camembert is partly the same molecule as in used nappies. You don’t confuse the two because of the context.”

analysis.tldr: A new AI startup has built a computer model that can identify and create smells, which could eventually change how Indian perfume, consumer goods, and security industries operate.
the_story: An AI startup called Osmo, founded in 2023 by Alex Wiltschko after leaving Google Brain, claims its artificial intelligence model has achieved human-level olfactory intelligence (the ability to detect, discriminate, and create smells).

To train the model, a team of around 30 human sniffers in New Jersey and about 70 data labelers overseas created a dataset of over 10 million human labels and 800 million scent tokens using chemical sensors.
Osmo's technology has already been used by major consumer goods companies like Procter & Gamble to design new fragrances, outperforming in-house human perfumers in tests.
The startup also worked with the Gates Foundation to identify mosquito-repelling molecules and collaborated with online marketplace StockX to spot counterfeit sneakers by testing material scents.

Critics like smell scientist Avery Gilbert and former consultant Michael Schmuker point out that the company relies heavily on human sensory panels and that human smell relies heavily on context, like confusing a tasty cheese with a dirty diaper due to identical molecules.
analysis.what_happened: An AI startup named Osmo has developed a computer model designed to understand and generate smells. Because computers cannot naturally smell, the company solved this by feeding its AI massive amounts of chemical data and descriptions from human sniffers, allowing the software to create custom fragrances and analyze scents like a human would.
analysis.analogy: It is like teaching a computer what colors look like by showing it millions of paint combinations, except instead of sight, the computer is learning how different chemical molecules mix together to create smells like 'peachy' or 'nutty'.
why_it_matters_india: AI smell technology is adopted by global consumer goods companies -> Indian consumer goods and cosmetics brands face pressure to adopt similar tech to stay competitive
Global firms use AI to create cheaper or more effective fragrances -> Indian manufacturing sectors for perfumes, soaps, and home care items may license or build similar AI tools
Security and health applications are developed using AI scent detection -> Indian airports and medical facilities might eventually explore scent-based threat or disease screening
Global beauty and tech trends shift toward digital olfaction -> Indian tech startups and R&D centers in the fragrance space face new benchmarks

impacts.target: FMCG (Fast-Moving Consumer Goods) stocks like Hindustan Unilever & ITC
impacts.rationale: If these major consumer goods companies adopt smell-matching AI to design better soaps and perfumes faster, it could boost their product appeal, though the direct financial impact right now is minimal.

watch_next: Whether more major consumer goods companies adopt Osmo's AI for commercial perfume lines
If competitor tech companies release open-source versions of smell AI models
analysis.caveats: This article discusses a single US-based startup making claims that are still met with skepticism by some independent scientists.

history.title: A state-encouraged bubble and a surprise devaluation
history.what: Chinese shares doubled in a year, partly on state media encouragement, then fell about 40% in three months. In August the central bank unexpectedly devalued the yuan, and world markets fell sharply over two days.
history.why: Retail investors, many with newly opened accounts and little experience, had bought heavily on margin loans. When prices turned, margin calls forced selling, which forced more margin calls. The devaluation then signalled that China's slowdown was worse than official figures admitted, which hit everyone selling into Chinese demand.
history.impact: Commodities collapsed — copper, iron ore and oil all fell hard, since China consumed roughly half the world's industrial metals. Emerging market currencies including the rupee weakened. Indian metal shares fell sharply despite nothing changing in India.
history.policy: Trading halts, a ban on large shareholders selling, state funds instructed to buy, and tighter capital controls to stop money leaving. Later, a managed and better-communicated currency mechanism.
history.consequence: It exposed the limits of administrative intervention in a market: the measures slowed the fall but damaged foreign investors' trust in Chinese market access for years. That trust deficit is part of why global money has been reallocating toward India since.
history.pattern: Retail leverage is the accelerant. A market where ordinary investors are buying with borrowed money does not correct gently, because the selling is involuntary. Margin data is one of the few genuinely predictive warnings.
history.india_echo: Worth watching Indian margin funding and futures-and-options participation, both of which have grown enormously since 2020. For that risk, 2015 China is the more relevant precedent than 2008 America.
history.watch_for: Rapid growth in new trading accounts alongside rising borrowed positions. That pair has preceded every retail-driven unwind.
